lead: A reverse-biased p–n junction turns absorbed light into current: each absorbed photon makes an electron–hole pair, and the junction field sweeps the pair out before it recombines. A plain PN diode collects light only in its thin depletion layer, so it is inefficient and slow. Putting a wide intrinsic (i) layer between the p and n sides gives the PIN photodiode, the standard detector of fiber links from 0.85 µm to 1.55 µm. This chapter covers how it collects carriers, the trade-off between efficiency, capacitance and speed, and the numbers a receiver designer works out.
prereq: You need quantum efficiency and responsivity from Detection principles.

sections.h3: Reverse bias turns photons into drift current

blocks.text: A PN photodiode is a p–n junction held in reverse bias. The reverse voltage widens the depletion region and makes its electric field strong. When a photon with energy hν ≥ E<sub>g</sub> is absorbed, it creates an electron–hole pair. If this happens inside the depletion region, the field separates the pair at once: the electron drifts to the n side and the hole to the p side. This drift of charge is the photocurrent, and it flows in the external circuit.

A pair created in the neutral p or n region feels almost no field. It moves only by slow diffusion and often recombines before it reaches the junction. Any carrier that does diffuse in arrives late and gives a slow tail on the pulse. So in a plain PN diode, with a depletion width of about a micrometre, much of the light is wasted and the response is slow.

blocks.where: η is the quantum efficiency; r is the fraction of light reflected at the surface; α is the absorption coefficient (in m⁻¹ or cm⁻¹); w is the width of the depleted layer. The factor (1 − r) is the light that enters, and (1 − e<sup>−αw</sup>) is the part of it absorbed within w. The formula assumes every pair made in w is collected.

sections.h3: The PIN structure widens the collecting region

blocks.text: A PIN photodiode places an undoped (intrinsic) i layer between a heavily doped p⁺ layer and an n⁺ layer. A small reverse bias depletes the whole i layer, so the field acts across its full width and almost all the light is absorbed where carriers are collected. Light enters through a thin p⁺ layer, kept thin so that little light is absorbed there, and an antireflection coating brings r down to a few percent. The i width is now chosen for the optics rather than set by doping.

How wide the i layer must be depends on α. InGaAs at 1.55 µm absorbs strongly (α ≈ 10⁴ cm⁻¹, so 1/α = 1 µm), and an i layer of 2 to 5 µm absorbs 86 % to 99 % of the light. Silicon at 0.85 µm absorbs weakly (α of the order of 10³ cm⁻¹ or less), so a silicon PIN needs an i layer of 20 to 50 µm and is slower.

items: Silicon covers 0.8–0.9 µm, with responsivity around 0.5–0.6 A/W.

Germanium and InGaAs cover 1.3 µm and 1.55 µm. A packaged InGaAs PIN typically gives about 0.9 to 1.0 A/W at 1.55 µm; the ideal (1 − r)(1 − e<sup>−αw</sup>) estimate is higher because it ignores light lost in the p⁺ layer and under the contacts.

blocks.text: A wide i layer lowers the junction capacitance, which helps speed, but carriers take longer to cross it, which hurts speed. The next section puts numbers on both.

sections.h3: Two bandwidth limits: transit time and RC

blocks.text: Carriers cross the i layer at the saturation velocity v<sub>sat</sub>, about 1 × 10⁵ m/s in silicon and about 6.5 × 10⁴ m/s for the slower carriers (holes) in InGaAs. The transit time is t<sub>tr</sub> = w/v<sub>sat</sub>. For light absorbed evenly across the layer, the current response falls by 3 dB at f<sub>tr</sub> ≈ 0.44/t<sub>tr</sub>. Some textbooks use the rougher estimate v<sub>sat</sub>/(2w) = 0.5/t<sub>tr</sub>; say which one you use.

The junction is also a parallel-plate capacitor, C = ε<sub>r</sub>ε<sub>0</sub>A/w, with ε<sub>0</sub> = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F/m and A the diode area. With the load resistor R<sub>L</sub> it forms a low-pass filter with corner f<sub>RC</sub> = 1/(2πR<sub>L</sub>C).
The two limits act together, so the diode's overall bandwidth is lower than either of them. The smaller of the two tells you which one to improve.

Design is a push and pull. A wider w raises η and lowers C (fRC rises), but ttr grows (ftr falls). A larger area A makes fiber alignment easy but raises C. The bias must be high enough to deplete the whole i layer and keep carriers at vsat. For a high-speed receiver, choose w so that both limits are well above the bandwidth needed, then accept the η that results. When even a good PIN gives too little current, internal gain helps: see Avalanche photodiodes.

examples.question: An InGaAs PIN photodiode for 1.55 µm has i-layer width w = 4 µm, absorption coefficient α = 1 × 10⁴ cm⁻¹, surface reflectivity r = 0.03, area A = 1 × 10⁻⁸ m² (a 100 µm × 100 µm square), relative permittivity ε<sub>r</sub> = 13.9 and load resistance R<sub>L</sub> = 50 Ω. The carriers cross at v<sub>sat</sub> = 6.5 × 10⁴ m/s. Find η and R, the transit time and f<sub>tr</sub>, the capacitance and f<sub>RC</sub>, and the overall bandwidth. Which limit controls?
steps: Same units for αw: w = 4 µm = 4 × 10⁻⁴ cm, so αw = (1 × 10⁴ cm⁻¹)(4 × 10⁻⁴ cm) = 4.0.
η = (1 − r)(1 − e<sup>−αw</sup>) = 0.97 × 0.9817 = 0.952. Responsivity R = ηλ/1.24 = 0.952 × 1.55/1.24 = 1.19 A/W (an ideal estimate; a packaged diode gives less).
Transit time: t<sub>tr</sub> = w/v<sub>sat</sub> = (4 × 10⁻⁶ m)/(6.5 × 10⁴ m/s) = 6.15 × 10⁻¹¹ s = 61.5 ps.

Overall: f<sub>3dB</sub> ≈ 1/√(1/7.15² + 1/10.35²) GHz = 5.88 GHz. The smaller limit is f<sub>tr</sub> = 7.15 GHz, so this diode is transit-time limited: a thinner i layer would make it faster, at some cost in η.
examples.answer: η = 0.952 (R ≈ 1.19 A/W), t<sub>tr</sub> = 61.5 ps, f<sub>tr</sub> = 7.15 GHz, C = 0.308 pF, f<sub>RC</sub> = 10.35 GHz, overall bandwidth about 5.9 GHz; transit time limits it.

traps: Thinking a thicker i layer is always better. It raises η and lowers C, but it lengthens the transit time and lowers f<sub>tr</sub>.
Dropping (1 − r). With r = 0.03, 3 % of the light is lost before any absorption.
Mixing units in αw: α in cm⁻¹ needs w in cm, α in m⁻¹ needs w in m. Mixing them gives an exponent 100 times wrong.
Reporting the smaller limit as the bandwidth. The two limits combine, so the real bandwidth (5.9 GHz in the example) is below both.
Forward biasing a photodiode. It must be reverse biased (or at zero bias); forward bias injects its own current and swamps the photocurrent.

quiz.q: What does the i in PIN stand for, and what does that layer do?
quiz.a: Intrinsic. The wide undoped i layer is fully depleted in reverse bias, so its field sweeps the electron–hole pairs made by light out as photocurrent.

quiz.q: Why do pairs made in the neutral p and n regions add little useful photocurrent?
quiz.a: They are outside the strong junction field. They move only by slow diffusion, many recombine on the way, and those that arrive come late and slow the pulse down.

quiz.q: A silicon PIN photodiode has surface reflectivity r = 0.05 and αw = 2.0. Find its quantum efficiency.
A designer doubles the i-layer width w and keeps the area and material the same. State the effect on η, C, t<sub>tr</sub>, f<sub>tr</sub> and f<sub>RC</sub>.
quiz.a: η rises, because αw doubles (for the example diode from 0.952 to 0.970). C halves, since C = εA/w. t<sub>tr</sub> doubles, since t<sub>tr</sub> = w/v<sub>sat</sub>. f<sub>tr</sub> halves. f<sub>RC</sub> doubles because C halves. The diode becomes more strongly transit-time limited.

quiz.q: Which detector material is usual at 1.55 µm, and what responsivity does a packaged device typically give?
Why is the p⁺ layer kept thin in a front-illuminated PIN photodiode?
quiz.a: Light enters through the p⁺ side. Pairs made in that undepleted layer are mostly lost, so a thin p⁺ layer lets more light reach the i layer, where collection happens.

quiz.q: An InGaAs PIN has w = 5 µm and v<sub>sat</sub> = 6.5 × 10⁴ m/s. Find the transit time and the transit-time bandwidth.

beyond: Not for the exam. Fast receivers use waveguide photodiodes and back-illuminated structures, which shorten the carriers' path without shortening the light's absorption path. Uni-travelling-carrier photodiodes let only the fast electrons cross the depleted layer. Germanium-on-silicon photodiodes bring 1.55 µm detection onto CMOS chips. Search next for "waveguide photodiode", "uni-travelling-carrier photodiode" and "Ge-on-Si photodetector".

figure.caption: The worked example's InGaAs PIN: light enters through the coating and the thin p⁺ layer, and its power falls as it is absorbed across the 4 µm i layer, so only 1.8 % is left at the far side. The field below is strong across the whole i layer, so each pair is swept out: electrons to n⁺, holes to p⁺.

spec.aria: Layer diagram: antireflection coating, thin p plus layer, wide i layer of 4 micrometres, n plus layer. A curve inside the i layer shows the light power falling from 0.97 of the input to 1.8 percent. Below, the electric field is near zero in p plus and n plus and high and flat across the i layer.
